posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: CRO at a financial firm validating the explainability problem in analytics — with high-value ICP prospects engaging — add the 'audit trail not just answer' framing without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is the new 'the model says so' — different technology, same accountability gap. Regulators don't want outputs, they want reasoning they can follow step by step. The real problem isn't AI in analytics, it's analytics tools that were never built to explain themselves in the first place. Wonder how many teams are quietly in the same position right now but haven't hit a regulator question yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the pain around trust, not tooling, and add the real insight nobody says out loud
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the problem. It's that the first time a number looked wrong — even slightly — everyone quietly went back to the spreadsheet they already trusted. And once that happens, you're not selling a tool anymore, you're selling confidence in a number, which is a completely different job. How long did it take before you figured out that's what you were actually fighting?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why usage is the real metric' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a cry for help dressed up as a strategy. The jump from 10% to 85% usage is the number nobody tracks but it's the only one that tells you if any of it was worth building. Most teams obsess over what's on the dashboard and never ask who's actually opening it. What made you pick those 5 — was it gut or did someone finally just admit what they were actually using?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at a retail brand is watching this thread — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, then add the sharper insight that the problem isn't self-service, it's that nobody defined the rules before handing out the tools
posts.draft_comment: The three definitions of revenue thing is so common it's almost a rite of passage. The issue usually isn't that people got access — it's that access came before alignment on what anything actually means. Self-service works fine when there's a shared language underneath it. Most orgs skip that part and wonder why the chaos follows.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucination as material risk with a CEO prospect engaged — validate the reframe from accuracy to security, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The reframe from accuracy issue to security issue is exactly right, and most analytics vendors aren't ready for that conversation. The problem is AI tools have been sold on speed and ease — 'get answers in seconds' — but nobody stress-tested what happens when a hallucinated number makes it into a board deck and drives a real decision. Trust in data has always been hard to build and easy to destroy. Who's actually holding AI analytics outputs accountable when something goes wrong?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the real dysfunction, add the 'who it was actually built for' insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number stings but honestly the bigger cost is the six months of 'we're still onboarding' before everyone quietly goes back to Excel. Most of these platforms were designed to impress a data team in a demo, not to get a COO an answer on a Tuesday morning without filing a ticket. The self-service promise only works if the person doing the serving and the person doing the asking are the same person — and in a 50-person company, they rarely are.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company nailing the real root cause of BI distrust — validate the culture diagnosis and add the layer about *why* culture breaks down around data in the first place
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter sets, one awkward CFO question — that's not a data problem, that's a trust problem dressed up as a data problem. And culture is the right call, but I'd push it one step further: the culture usually breaks because nobody agreed on *who owns the definition* before the dashboard went live. The tool gets blamed because the governance conversation never happened. How long had those three versions been running before the quarterly review surfaced it?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' adoption failure — validate that insight and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is pretty honest of you to share. That 'nobody knows what to ask' problem is the thing nobody wants to say out loud — because it means the investment in the tool was the easy part, and the hard part is that most people don't actually know what they need to know about their own business. Shadow AI filling that gap with ChatGPT on phones is a symptom of the same thing, just less controlled. What does your team think the blocker actually is — the questions, or the data people are supposed to be asking questions about?
